t: Maximum Number of People That Can Be Caught in Tag - Greedy Matching With Two Pointers
o: Each "it" person at index i can catch at most one non-it person whose index lies in [i - dist, i + dist], so maximizing catches is a bipartite matching problem: left side the its, right side the non-its, with an edge whenever indices are within dist. In Example 1 the its at indices 1 and 3 have wide windows under dist = 3, but each catches only one person, so index 4 stays uncaught and the answer is 2. Example 2 has no non-it people at all, and Example 3 has a lone non-it out of everyone's reach - both answer 0. With n up to 100000 we need something better than generic matching; the interval structure of the edges admits a linear greedy.
k: Model the game as bipartite matching between "it" people and non-it people with edges |i - j| <= dist.
Scanning its left to right while grabbing the leftmost still-uncaught reachable non-it is exchange-safe: any optimal assignment can be rearranged to match this greedy without losing pairs.
A forward-only pointer over non-it indices makes every step O(1) amortized.
w: State the greedy and its exchange argument in an interview; mention augmenting-path matching only if asked about generalizations such as weighted catches or per-person distances. Pitfalls: advance the non-it pointer past people below i - dist permanently (no later window reaches back to the left), but when the next candidate exceeds i + dist leave the pointer in place since a later "it" has a window shifted right that may still reach them; also mind the inclusive endpoints and teams containing only its or only non-its. Follow-ups: each catcher takes up to k people, per-person dist values, or players arranged on a circle.

a.n: Approach 1: Bipartite Matching With Augmenting Paths
a.i: Translate the game literally into bipartite matching and run Kuhn's algorithm: for each non-it person, try to find an "it" within dist who is either unmatched or can re-route their current catch onto someone else via a depth-first alternating search. This directly models maximality reasoning and generalizes beyond interval edges, but its running time is quadratic-scale on this input size.
s: Collect the indices of its and non-its separately.
For each non-it person j, run an augmenting DFS with a fresh visited set over the its.
In the DFS, visit each it t within dist of j that is not yet visited this round.
If t is unmatched, or the non-it currently matched to t can itself be re-routed, match t to j and report success.
Count successful augmentations as the answer.
a.t: O(V * E) - up to n augmenting rounds, each scanning up to n candidate its through recursive re-routing; too slow at n = 10^5
a.sp: O(n) - index lists, the match array, and per-round visited marks

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy Sweep With a Forward-Only Pointer
a.i: Process its in increasing index order and give each one the leftmost still-uncaught non-it inside its window. The exchange argument makes this optimal: if an optimal solution assigned the current it to some farther person q', while the leftmost candidate q is also feasible here, swapping assignments keeps every pair legal because windows only shift rightward for later its. A pointer over non-it indices never moves backward: people below i - dist are permanently out of reach (future windows start even further right), while a person beyond i + dist simply waits for a later it.
s: List the indices of all non-it people.
Sweep its in ascending index order with pointer p at the first uncaught non-it.
Advance p past everyone with index < i - dist; they are unreachable forever.
If nonit[p] <= i + dist, catch them (increment answer and p); otherwise leave p for later its.
The count of successful catches is the answer.
a.t: O(n) - each of the two sweeps moves forward at most n steps in total
a.sp: O(n) - the list of non-it indices (O(1) extra beyond that)
